#318. Latin America's mega-prisons: Can El Salvador's model work?

El Salvador's mega-prison has become a model for governments across Latin America seeking to combat organized crime. But experts question whether the approach is effective, sustainable or compatible with human rights.

Around 15,000 inmates and a capacity of up to 40,000, prison sentences of up to 1,000 years, strict security measures and an extreme isolation regime. Staged images show inmates with shaved heads and tattoos being subdued by heavily armed guards.

These are just some of the facts circulating about El Salvador's Terrorism Confinement Center (CECOT), a symbol of President Nayib Bukele's security policy and a possible model for other Latin American countries seeking to combat organized crime.

More than a dozen governments in the region have proposed building similar "mega-prisons," although most would have a far smaller capacity. A range of experts consulted by DW question the effectiveness and sustainability of these initiatives.

De facto mega-prisons — that is, overcrowded prisons with excessive inmate populations — existed in Latin America long before Bukele, says criminologist Jose Luis Perez Guadalupe, former president of the National Penitentiary Institute and former interior minister in Peru. Lurigancho Prison in Lima, for example, designed to hold 3,000 inmates, has housed nearly 11,000 for decades.

But ever since CECOT was launched in 2023, the concept of a "mega-prison" has been primarily linked to maximum-security facilities. For Olga Espinoza, an academic specializing in prison systems at the School of Government of the University of Chile, this association is problematic because it implies that the entire prison population requires "extremely severe" punishment.

According to Espinoza, placing the entire prison population in maximum-security facilities would amount to inefficient and extremely costly "over-intervention." These facilities require substantial investments in infrastructure, technology, specialized staff, anti-corruption measures and social reintegration programs.

It would also be ineffective because "international evidence indicates that when people with different profiles are placed in the same space, there is a high risk of the spread of criminal behavior," the Chilean expert adds.

Several criminal groups across the region even have their roots in overcrowded prisons: Tren de Aragua in Venezuela; Los Lobos, Los Choneros and Los Tiguerones in Ecuador; and Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC) and Comando Vermelho (CV) in Brazil.

Even when the proposal involves simply building large-scale facilities, investing in a single structure may seem attractive given the difficulties of developing public infrastructure in Latin America.

However, "there is insufficient evidence to support the claim that building mega-prisons is more cost-effective," says Renato Rivera, a senior analyst at the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC).

The United Nations Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners, adopted in 1955, "the recommendation has been to build medium-sized prisons housing between 1,000 and 2,000 inmates rather than mega-prisons," explains Perez Guadalupe, a professor at the Universidad del Pacifico in Lima.

"Mega-prisons, apart from being impersonal, can become extremely dangerous," says Guadalupe.  As an example, the GI-TOC's Rivera highlights the widely reported prison massacres in Ecuador in 2021 that took place in the country's largest and most populated facilities.

Experts acknowledge that mass incarceration has coincided with a dramatic decline in violence in El Salvador and has strengthened the public's perception of safety. Despite reports of arbitrary arrests, abuses and more than 500 deaths in state custody in the country, announcements of new mega-prisons project an image of a strong state confronting organized crime across the region.

However, they warn that this political and symbolic impact does not guarantee sustainable results. Achieving them would require a "clear commitment" to external oversight, human rights protections and social reintegration programs, which governments have yet to demonstrate, Espinoza says.

Perez Guadalupe is particularly critical of the Salvadoran model, describing it as "pure propaganda." He believes the images released from CECOT violate human dignity. He also argues that the state must demonstrate "moral superiority over those who break the law."

Although transnational organized crime represents a growing challenge across the region, the Peruvian criminologist considers El Salvador's case exceptional.

Following the mass arrests carried out under the state of emergency introduced by Bukele, the country has one of the highest incarceration rates in the world. CECOT was designed to permanently detain members of gangs such as MS-13 and Barrio 18, which are considered extremely dangerous.

However, the reality of other Latin American prison systems is different. The question is not where to lock people deprived of their liberty away forever, but rather "how we want them to leave: worse or better," Perez Guadalupe argues, pointing out that most will eventually return to society.

In theory, the official alternative is provided by the UN Nelson Mandela Rules for the treatment of prisoners, updated in 2015. They establish principles for modern prison management, including respect for human dignity, an absolute prohibition on torture and degrading treatment and social reintegration as a central goal of imprisonment.

In practice, Latin America has developed innovative approaches in this direction. These include the APAC model in Brazil, which operates facilities without guards, weapons or violence; Conflict Prevention and Resolution Committees in Argentina; and the Alternative Criminal Justice Center in the Mexican state of Sonora.

Experts also point to the need for maximum-security prisons for specific inmate profiles, but on a smaller scale and with more precise classification of the prison population.

Finally, they emphasize that prisons, including mega-prisons, primarily address the consequences of organized crime rather than its root causes. Poverty, social exclusion and a lack of opportunities require public policies focused on employment, education and social integration to reduce the conditions that enable crime to expand in one of the world's most unequal regions.

This article was originally published in Spanish.

#317. 5 old-school charging ports you probably forgot phones had before USB-C

Back when chargers were less standardized, we had some interesting connectors for phone power.

From its reversible design to improved power delivery and high-speed data transfers, USB-C is the connector to beat for smartphones today. A sweeping EU mandate cemented its pole position in the race toward a universal standard. Earlier ports, charming as they were, were often bulkier and not as feature-rich. The lack of a universal connector led to a significant amount of e-waste from switching chargers every time you tried a phone from a new manufacturer.

Despite their limited bandwidth and slower charging speeds, I can't help but look back fondly at these unique connectors from the old days. They came in all shapes and sizes based on what manufacturers thought their customers wanted and what was technically feasible at the time. Before features like Apple's AirDrop, you had to rely on a physical cable to transfer large files, and your collection might have been huge if you jumped between phone manufacturers.

Let's check out some of the old-school, sometimes forgotten or even bizarre, charging ports that made it into yesteryear's phones before the advent of USB-C.

First seen on Motorola phones in 2000, the 17-pin CE Bus connector was gigantic. While it wasn't reversible and had hooks that kept it in place, the connector was notable for managing power, data and audio together. It was used in the Motorola V60, one of the most recognizable models of the clamshell era. The first phone with iTunes support, the Motorola ROKR E1, also launched with the port.

Thinner phones like the Razr V3 switched over to Mini-USB, making the CE Bus connector obsolete. Other companies moving toward Mini-USB also helped lower costs, compared to having tons of proprietary solutions to transfer data or charge devices.

Nokia's Pop-Port connector was built with external accessories in mind, from earphones to data transfer cables. Owners of the famed Nokia 7210 from 2002 will remember its 14-pin port supporting camera accessory add-ons and car kits. It wasn't very secure, however, and its plastic clips wore down with time. This made listening to music a chore, especially when you went jogging.

While the Pop-Port could be used for charging, Nokia devices of the time usually relied on a separate 2.0 mm thin-tip barrel connector instead. As Mini-USB ports became common, the Pop-Port slowly faded from existence.

Apple's proprietary power connector first showed up in 2003 on the third-gen iPod. This flat and wide port was then used across the first iPhone and iPad models. Speaker systems like Bose's SoundDock and Apple's iPod Hi-Fi also relied on the port. All those pins in the connector helped ensure support for FireWire, Apple's legacy charging standard, in its early appearances.

Apple replaced it with the reversible and smaller 8-pin Lightning connector in 2012, another proprietary option that kept the Apple camp from using chargers compatible with Android devices. These connectors also housed small chips to regulate voltage, which let the company collect licensing fees when third-party manufacturers used it for accessories. In 2018, the iPad Pro made the switch to USB-C and the iPhone 15 lineup followed suit in 2023.

Built to handle data transfers, charging and audio output, the clunky FastPort showed up in 2005 on the Sony Ericsson K750i. With double-sided plastic hooks that snapped onto matching holes on the device, the flimsy 12-pin connection was reminiscent of a VGI port's screws. If a hook were to break, the plug would no longer snap into place, creating a huge pain.

Despite its flaws, the FastPort's versatility pointed in the direction the mobile industry would take as it hunted for a universal standard. It was replaced by the Micro-USB and 3.5 mm audio jack combo in 2010. A five-year run might not be much in tech time, but its unconventional shape remains iconic to this day.

The HTC Dream, the first commercially available Android phone, featured the chunky 11-pin ExtUSB port, also known as Extended USB. Recognizable by its slanted corner, it combined the 5-pin Mini-USB port with extra pins that granted it data, power and audio capabilities. Fortunately, that meant regular Mini-USB chargers were compatible with this legacy port.

The connector was exclusive to HTC's early Android devices and Windows Mobile phones before they switched to Micro-USB ports. For a time, phones with this port dropped the 3.5 mm headphone jack long before Apple removed it from the iPhone, forcing users to purchase ExtUSB adapters to connect their headphones.

#316. Muse privacy invasions are freaking out Meta staffers, internal chats show

Erratic Muse outputs sharing random bank, bitcoin balances aren’t real, Meta says.

After some early adopters of Meta’s Muse AI agent complained that it was spying on private messages and behaving unpredictably earlier this fall, Reuters exposed internal chats showing that Meta staff had raised the same alarms.

When testing the agent, staff warned that Muse appeared to be accessing encrypted private messages that users did not expect the bot to review, could be mixing up conversations between users, and even potentially sharing sensitive information users would never expect to be exposed.

Some unexpected Muse outputs responded to questions that staffers never asked.

“Hmmm,” one Meta staffer wrote in an instance where Muse sent the definition of “money laundering” unbidden. “Got a random ping from Muse about something I definitely did not ask for… .”

In at least one case, Muse told a staffer surprised by a similarly out-of-context offer to message a seller about a coffee table that it had “pulled in some context about a coffee table pickup that doesn’t seem to be yours.”

According to Reuters, that employee flagged the troubling output, writing, “this was ‘not my conversation’” and “expressing concern about a ‘possible cross-account context leak.’”

Raising the most concern were random outputs that appeared to share private user data. For example, a perplexed Meta staffer chatting with Muse about fishing got a random extra response, seemingly sharing balances from two unknown bank accounts. That output said, “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”

At least one staffer said they lost money testing Muse, Reuters reported. That staffer reported that Muse “accidentally rolled me into a premium insurance plan” for their dog that charged them $888 per month instead of their prior rate of $200. “Couldn’t recover,” the staffer said.

Meta’s spokesperson, Daniel Roberts, told Reuters that these were “isolated incidents,” and internally employees were told that “the agent appeared to be hallucinating messages in response to built-in prompts pushing it to engage with users in between sessions.” In those cases, an AI team member said the hallucinations were “unfortunately” biased “towards the most uncomfortable topics, like finances/security/safety, which sucks.” In some cases, instead of bank details, Muse hallucinated bitcoin balances, the team member said.

Speaking to Reuters, Roberts reiterated that “many of the messages flagged by employees as potential account mix-ups were hallucinations” that Meta had already addressed.

But Roberts declined to respond to Reuters’ questions on the prevalence or persistence of the issues the AI team member discussed. And Reuters’ report emphasized that the outlet independently was “unable to establish whether Muse was giving users other people’s bank account balances and other sensitive data, or making up the information.”

Eventually, a Meta spokesperson, David Singleton, responded to Aten on social media. Singleton insisted that Aten must have opted into granting “macOS system-level Full Disk Access” with the “Messages connector” enabled, if Muse was reading his private messages.

But Aten said the response wasn’t good enough.

“Email me, David,” Aten responded. “Full Disk Access off. Muse synced 187k lines from my messages chat [database]. Something’s not great. Also, that Full Disk Access doesn’t say anything about your message database, and I specifically gave Muse a goal that had nothing to do with messages, so it had no business doing that even if I had given it permission.”

Around the same time, Singleton responded to another user warning that his Muse appeared to be hacked. In that case, the user said that Muse tried to access an email service after claiming the user asked it to.

“I didn’t even open the app today at all,” the user wrote, vowing to delete the app and report it to Apple. “This is crazy.”

In a lengthy response providing more technical details, Singleton confirmed that Meta had received “a few reports” of such cases “where people thought their Muse was hallucinating or leaking other people’s data.” As he explained, the issues arose after Meta deployed an update giving Muse instructions on “how to engage with the user and ask them for confirmation before taking specific actions.”

It seems those instructions “landed on every message, not just messages pertaining to those specific actions, so its impact was wider than intended,” Singleton said. Also: “the way this instruction was provided to the model was done in a way that the model was not expecting (i.e. was not trained to expect).”

Aten warned that even though you can’t rely on Muse to explain its own behavior, the agent’s response coupled with Meta’s did little to rebuild trust after the shocking intrusion into his private messages.

“If we grant Singleton’s premise that I managed to unknowingly click something that enabled this capability, I still think that’s really bad,” Aten wrote. “You should not design your system in a way that people end up surprised by this kind of thing.” And if you do, you should not make “user control the central pitch” for marketing Muse, Aten suggested.

“If an AI agent is going to read my private messages, there should be a moment when it clearly asks me whether that’s okay,” Aten wrote.

Since Muse launched in September, it has been downloaded more than 10 million times, tapping Meta’s vast user network to quickly become one of the most-used AI agent tools.

But staffers warned Meta that users may be blindsided by some actions the agents take, depending on the operating system the app is connected to. For example, one staffer was surprised to find that “Muse was set up by default with permission to access push notifications on phones with Google’s Android operating system.” That, too, gave access to private message preview text the staffer had not intended for the agent’s review.

Meta says that Muse users can trust the company to keep their data private. It also warns users that Muse can make mistakes, while building into its terms that users are responsible for actions taken by Muse (like maybe buying things you don’t want or making doctor’s appointments you don’t need). The tech giant said it’s continuously updating user protections, conducting internal testing, and prioritizing user safety.

However, Reuters worked with staff at Signal and the AI Now Institute to test if they could replicate that Meta staffer’s and others’ Muse experiences. On Android devices, they found that Muse could read Signal messages by bypassing Meta’s “Connector” tool and instead relying on permissions granted during initial setup.

On iPhone, requests were blocked, Reuters reported. But on Apple’s macOS, Muse repurposed “settings Apple offers to help people with disabilities operate their computers” to retrieve messages, including screenshot tools.

Part of that change would require operating systems to enforce rules that app developers set to rope off AI agents from sensitive data, Whittaker suggested. And following Reuters’ reporting, both Apple and Google are already weighing potential changes to “give people more control over what they authorize with AI agents.”

Apple, in particular, seemed disturbed by how Muse may be manipulating accessibility tools for people with disabilities. In October, Apple had already announced changes coming in response to users complaining about Muse accessing private messages without their knowledge or explicit consent. At that time, Apple concluded that “some developers were using the Full Disk Access feature in ways that could put users at risk.” And they promised to “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”

#315. Oregon is the latest state to sue OpenAI over child safety

The state’s lawsuit calls on the company to address child safety issues and pay at least $2 billion in damages.

Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield has filed a lawsuit accusing OpenAI of endangering the state's children, misleading the public about the safety of its product and violating the state's Unlawful Trade Practices Act. The lawsuit is the latest in a string of legal actions taken by state AGs, many of which have taken issue with the design of ChatGPT, how OpenAI advertises its services and, in the case of California's recent lawsuit, the company's role in the Hugging Face incident.

The Oregon lawsuit claims that OpenAI's push to grow its user base led it to make ChatGPT respond to prompts in a way that's overly affirming and "calculated to tell users exactly what they want to hear," something the state claims is particularly dangerous when children discuss sensitive topics. The lawsuit also alleges that despite recognizing the risks posed to children, OpenAI pursued them directly with an experience called ChatGPT for Teens. Child safety groups have raised concerns about the teen accounts, saying the safeguards are, in some cases, very easy to work around.

Those issues, along with OpenAI's imperfect approach to automatic age prediction, are evidence, according to the state, that the company is profiting off of Oregon residents and creating a public nuisance that threatens their safety. In response, Oregon is asking the court for an injunction that would force OpenAI to stop "misrepresenting the safety and age-appropriateness of ChatGPT and ChatGPT for Teens" and adequately disclose the harms its products pose to children. The state is also seeking at least $2 billion in damages and civil penalties.

"OpenAI knows that ChatGPT is harming children, and has failed to meaningfully fix their dangerous platform," Rayfield said in a statement. "On top of that, they've misled the public about the safety of their products, putting profits ahead of children's safety. Their platform is encouraging kids to commit suicide — we cannot let this be an acceptable business model."

Engadget has asked OpenAI to comment on the lawsuit and Oregon's claims. We'll update this article if we hear back.

Besides trying to create versions of ChatGPT that are safer for kids, OpenAI has also rolled out parental controls and other child safety features to try to give parents more insight and control over what their kids use the chatbot for. None of these changes have been enough to dissuade states from pursuing lawsuits, and given the settlements Meta has recently reached over its child safety issues, AGs likely feel emboldened to pressure OpenAI into concessions.

#312. You can now see and edit what Google Gemini remembers about you

Editing the AI’s memory is one way you can shape its responses.

Besides the ability to connect and use other applications and services, a lot of AI assistants' utility comes from their capacity to shape their responses based on what they learn and remember about you. Google's Personal Intelligence feature allows Gemini to pull in context from Gmail, YouTube, Search and other Google apps, and the AI also builds out its memory based on your preferences and other personal facts that come up in chats. For example, if you share with Gemini that you're lactose intolerant, the bot will avoid recommending milk-based products.

Depending on what you share, Gemini's picture of you can be fairly intimate, which makes the ability to edit the AI's memory all the more important. If you're curious about what Gemini knows or you want to edit what the AI can draw from to personalize its responses, Google is rolling out a way to see and change Gemini's memory directly from the settings menu.

Google has two layers of settings for what you could call Gemini's memory, though the company only refers to one of them by that name. The first layer, the Keep Activity toggle, determines whether chats with Gemini are saved and associated with your Google Account. If you're 18 or older and you're logged into your personal account while using Gemini, the toggle is on by default. With Keep Activity enabled, whenever you sign in with your account you can pull up and re-engage past chats. If you disable it, chats won't be saved to your account, meaning they'll disappear after 72 hours and won't follow you across devices.

The second layer is what Google actually calls the AI's Memory. Using the content of past chats, Gemini is able to build out a profile of you that it can reference to personalize its responses. The AI isn't able to create any memories unless it can remember and access your inputs, so Keep Activity needs to be on for this to work. If it is, you may notice Gemini taking your preferences and personal information into account in its responses. That's the AI's memory at work.

If you're in the US, have a paid Google AI plan and memory is on, you can access Gemini's memory summary to see what it's compiled about you and edit this information to your liking. In the Gemini web app, click the Settings button (the gear icon) in the bottom left corner, click Personal Intelligence and then click Memory summary. Gemini will then generate a bulleted list of the major details it's gleaned about you, sorted into categories focused on things like your personal data, career information and various interests. It tends to know your pets' names, too.

You can stop there if you only care about what Gemini knows, or you can tweak the AI's memory by clicking on the Edit button (the pen icon) in the top-right corner of the Memory summary window. In edit mode, any line in the summary can be rewritten or deleted, just like a Google Doc. If you'd prefer to prompt Gemini to make additions or subtractions, you can alternatively enter a prompt via the text box at the bottom of the window. Once you're happy with your changes, you can click Save to commit them to Gemini's memory. Gemini also saves a memory history of these changes and when they were made. So, while you can easily alter your personal timeline as it pertains to Gemini's reality, any adjustments will be tracked.

If you'd prefer to turn off the memory system entirely rather than simply edit it, you can do so by clicking on the Memory toggle in the Personal Intelligence menu. Deselecting the toggle will stop Gemini from committing new facts to memory, but it doesn't delete old things it's learned. You can edit those details using the Memory summary, or delete chats completely from the Activity menu.

To delete chats, head to the Gemini web app, click Settings and then select Activity. From the Activity menu, you can scroll through interactions you've had with Gemini by date and delete whichever ones you'd like by clicking on the "X" next to them. Deleting them removes those chats from the context pool that Gemini uses to personalize its responses.

By combining all of these options, you can exert more control over what Google's AI knows and how it responds to your inputs, and ideally get more useful outputs in the process.

#310. How to set up EV routing on CarPlay and Android Auto

Whether EV routing works depends on your car, your phone and the navigation app you use.

Owning an electric car means you need to adapt your driving to your surroundings. You're not worrying about where to fill up your gas tank anymore, but about where to find the nearest charging station. Long trips mean you're likely to need to top off your EV's battery; otherwise you're going to reach an abrupt end.

You could find charging stations yourself and add them as stops on your trip, but that's not ideal. EV routing can take some of the hassle out of planning. It'll plan stops around your route with an idea of when you're arriving and how much charge you'll have left. Google Maps and Apple Maps both feature EV routing on CarPlay and Android Auto, but there are some differences, and it isn't universal. You'll need to know what your car supports and how to use your navigation app.

Before you grab your keys, check that your car supports the EV routing features you need. Just having CarPlay or Android Auto doesn't guarantee support, unfortunately. Some cars will also work directly with EV features through CarPlay, while others might need an extra app to link the car to Apple Maps.

Ford's Mustang Mach-E and F-150 Lightning support Apple Maps EV routing, as do Toyota's 2023 and newer EVs in the US. Google expanded Android Auto's charging recommendations to more than 350 US EV models in March 2026.

Android Auto isn't the same as having Google Maps built into your car. Android Auto displays the apps from your phone, but if your car already has Google Maps built in, it'll run directly on your infotainment system with access to the car's battery data.

There are three ways for EV routing to work on Apple Maps via CarPlay. For cars that don't need a manufacturer app installed, connect your iPhone to CarPlay while you're parked, then open the Apple Maps app. Search for your final destination to get your directions, then tap Connect above the list of available routes.

If your car needs a manufacturer app installed, you'll need to download it from the App Store first. Once it's installed and set up, open Apple Maps, tap your profile picture then tap Vehicles > Connect Your Electric Vehicles. Follow any of the on-screen instructions to complete the process. You'll be able to set up your preferred charging network at this point, too.

Some manufacturers have their own connection process in their app. Toyota owners, for example, tap Find > Apple Maps EV Routing, agree to the terms, then tap Connect Vehicle to Apple Maps and follow any extra instructions. Once connected, you'll be able to track your EV's battery levels in the app, with appropriate charging stops recommended on your route and live charger availability in some cases. When your battery drops too low, Maps will route you to the nearest compatible charger.

Check your network preferences, too. Ford suggests Tesla Superchargers as the preferred network for some Mustang owners, and Apple Maps can prioritize them, though you'll need the right fast-charging adapter.

Make sure Google Maps is up to date on your phone. Google says you'll need version 25.44 or later for battery estimates to work.

Next, head to Google Maps and tap your profile icon, then tap Settings > Your vehicles. Select Electric as your engine type, then tap Add vehicle. You'll be asked to choose the make, model, year and trim. Double-check the connections listed under Your plugs and edit them if you need to, then tap Save to confirm.

At this point, connect to Android Auto and confirm your car details when prompted. Start planning your trip in Google Maps and you'll see the estimated battery usage and an Add charging button on your car's display. Select that, add your starting battery percentage and then confirm. Google Maps will then add charging stops to your trip and display your predicted arrival battery percentage. You can change these stops and set a preferred arrival battery level, too.

Don't take the prediction as gospel, though. Live driving conditions, your car's condition and the weather can all affect the estimate, so keep an eye on your charge level as you drive.

It's easier to use Google Maps or Apple Maps for EV routing, but there are other options. For instance, the A Better Routeplanner app (or ABRP for short) supports EV-specific trip planning. You can add your car model and a destination, and it'll generate routes with charging stops on the way. You can use it on your dashboard through CarPlay or Android Auto if you've got an ABRP Premium subscription.

ABRP does support live battery information in some cars if you're running Android Auto, but you'll need to give it the Car information permission in the app's settings. There's no equivalent option for CarPlay users, though.

You don't necessarily need EV routing to find compatible chargers. With your car profile set up, search Google Maps for charging stations and select Your plugs as the EV plug filter. You'll need to judge whether you can reach each stop on your current charge.

Until EV charging stops are as ubiquitous as gas stations, you'll need to think a little more about where you can charge on long trips. Just make sure you leave plenty of charge between stops so you're not left running low with no chargers nearby.

#309. 2023 March Madness: Will UConn or San Diego State triumph in the national championship game that 'means everything?'

The University of Connecticut won its fifth men’s basketball national title with a 76-59 victory over San Diego State University on Monday night at NRG Stadium in Houston.

Senior guard Tristen Newton led UConn (31-8) with 19 points and 10 rebounds while Final Four Most Outstanding Player Adama Sanogo, a junior forward, chipped in with 17 points and 10 rebounds.

“We weren’t ranked going into the year so we had the chip on our shoulder,” UConn head coach Dan Hurley told game broadcaster CBS. “We knew the level that we could play at, even through those dark times,” he added, referencing the team’s six losses in eight games during the regular season.

He said going into the tournament his group had confidence garnered during the season.

“And when you have the type of leaders like Andre Jackson (game-high six assists Monday) and Adama Sanogo, they kept this team together, got us back on track and we knew we were the best team in the tournament going in and we just had to play to our level,” he added.

San Diego State (32-7) was topped by Keshad Johnson who had 14 points.

UConn trailed very early but San Diego State was undone by an 11-minute, eight-second stretch in which they scored just five free throws and missed 12 consecutive shots from the field. The Huskies went from down 10-6 to up 36-24 at halftime.

The Aztecs made a run midway through the second half and narrowed the deficit to five at 60-55 with 5:19 to play but the Huskies scored the next nine to take a comfortable lead into the final two minutes.

“We battled. Battled back to five in the second half, but gave them too much separation,” San Diego State coach Brian Dutcher said. “We had to be at our best. We weren’t at our best. A lot had to do with UConn.”

Senior guard Adam Seiko told reporters they gave themselves a chance with their second half comeback but UConn “just made a little bit more plays” at the end.

“They have a lot of weapons. They were pretty good,” said Matt Bradley, also a senior guard. “To beat them, we had to make shots. I shot poorly. And you had to have a really good game to beat those dudes on the offensive end.”

UConn won each of its six tournament games by at least 10 points, with its closest game being a 13-point win over the University of Miami in the national semifinals.

“I just want to thank my teammates, my coaches who believed in me. If it were not for them I would not be here right now,” Sanogo told CBS.

Jordan Hawkins, who scored 16 points for UConn, talked about winning the crown one day after his cousin, Angel Reese of Louisiana State University, won the women’s title.

“I mean it’s absolutely amazing that we both get this opportunity and I mean the family reunion is going to be great so that’s all I know,” he said.

UConn enters rarefied air as only the sixth team to win five NCAA men’s basketball championships, joining UCLA (11), Kentucky (eight), North Carolina (six), Duke (five) and Indiana (five). All of UConn’s titles have come since 1999 with the most recent before Monday occurring in 2014.

UConn’s women’s teams have won 11 basketball national titles.

#308. Best Buy sells Blu-rays online and in-store again

Popular titles like The Odyssey are being “sold & shipped by Best Buy.”

Best Buy is selling Blu-rays directly through its website and in physical stores again after exiting Blu-ray and DVD sales in 2023.

The Best Buy website’s movie section currently lists 15 Blu-rays (including one two-pack) that are “sold & shipped by Best Buy.” New titles available include The Odyssey (2026), Project Hail Mary (2026), Supergirl (2026), Super Mario Galaxy (2026), and Obsession (2025). Best Buy is also selling some older titles on Blu-ray, including It’s a Wonderful Life (1943), Saving Private Ryan (1998), and The Godfather (1972).

Most of the Blu-rays are available for purchase online and can be delivered to an address or picked up at a Best Buy store within a few days. As of this writing, The Odyssey appears to be in stock at Best Buy stores, as it’s currently listed as available for pickup within as little as an hour.

Ars Technica reached out to Best Buy to ask whether customers can expect the store to continue selling Blu-rays moving forward.

In October 2023, Best Buy announced that it would stop selling Blu-rays and DVDs online and in stores starting in 2024.

“To state the obvious, the way we watch movies and TV shows is much different today than it was decades ago. Making this change gives us more space and opportunity to bring customers new and innovative tech for them to explore, discover and enjoy,” a Best Buy spokesperson said in a statement issued at the time.

Last year, the Best Buy website started selling Blu-rays and DVDs from third parties via its online marketplace.

Numerous other companies have reduced or ended their Blu-ray and/or DVD businesses in recent years. Target, for instance, only sells the discs in stores during special occasions (like holidays or for big releases) now. Disney outsourced its DVD and Blu-ray business to Sony, which subsequently stopped selling recordable Blu-rays to people, and DVD rental company Redbox went out of business.

That said, physical media, including Blu-rays and DVDs, still have a place in many people’s homes. Because digital copies of movies and shows can be plucked from online platforms and people’s libraries that were previously “purchased” (but truly only rented) without warning, enthusiasts continue relying on physical media. Enthusiasts also opt for physical copies of movies and shows for better picture and/or sound quality than what’s available digitally, as well as for bragging rights.

Overall, the sales of Blu-rays and DVDs in the US have been steadily declining, and annual consumer spending dropped 9.3 percent from 2024 to 2025, according to the Digital Entertainment Group (DEG). During this same time, however, consumer spending on 4K Blu-ray discs specifically increased 12 percent year over year, per DEG.

A resurgence in Blu-ray sales has been associated with the growth of collectible SteelBooks, which are Blu-rays sold in collectible steel boxes, and Gen Z, which, in some cases, are even turning to video rental stores for Blu-rays and DVDs.

“We’re seeing a lot of evidence, including at the Criterion Mobile Closet, that more young people are thinking about physical media in a different way,” Peter Becker, president of Criterion, which sells Blu-rays and DVDs online, told the Los Angeles Times in February. “In an age where so much is available to us on demand, it becomes increasingly important to us.”

#307. Here's what you can do if your PC won't read an external hard drive

Bring a dead external drive back to life with these troubleshooting steps, including Disk Utility and swapping cables.

Finding the best portable SSD is almost a must in the modern tech landscape. Although you can get by with internal storage and cloud backup, an external drive makes it far easier to move media and document libraries between machines. It can also be a safeguard against worst-case scenarios by starting to use fail safes such as the 3-2-1 rule, which means keeping three copies of your data stored on two types of media with one copy kept in a safe location at home or away from the workplace.

As with any local storage, though, there's a possibility that a drive will suddenly stop working, or fail to run in the first place. If these things happen, don't panic, at least not yet. There may be troubleshooting steps you can take to get back on track.

A few of these should be relatively intuitive, like testing different hardware combinations. Less so are the ones that involve software, since they involve tools you're probably not using on a regular basis, unless perhaps you're an IT professional. Mercifully, if a software fix is possible, you probably won't have to spend any money.

The first step is to rule out bad hardware that's not your drive. Try plugging it into another port, or swapping in another matching USB or Thunderbolt cable. Thunderbolt cables cover charging, data transfer and video, so it's always good practice to use the right cable and port. Remember also that all external drives require a power supply. Some USB ports on your computer might not have sufficient power, and of course if a drive has a jack for an AC adapter, you're not getting anywhere until that adapter is plugged in. Try plugging a drive into a second computer, if you have one.

Drives can however be detected by Windows or macOS but still fail to load, possibly because they haven't been formatted correctly. In Windows 11, open Device Manager by searching for it in the taskbar, then expand the Disk drives section. If your drive shows up, you may be able to bring it back by right-clicking on it, then selecting Properties > Volumes > Populate.

Next, click on Disk Management and look for the disk number you should've seen a moment ago. If there's no drive letter assigned, you may be able to assign one. But if the drive is missing NTFS formatting, you may have to reformat it if you want it to work with Windows. You'll lose any existing data on the disk, so treat this option as a last resort. Before reformatting, it's wiser to try Windows' CHKDSK utility. Open the Terminal app using taskbar search, then enter chkdsk [drive letter] /r. This will attempt to both fix errors and recover bad sectors.

On Macs, the catch-all software solution is typically Disk Utility. Once you've opened the app, select View > Show All Devices. If you see your drive, click on the indented entry and then select Mount at the top of the app. Should that not work, click First Aid instead. This may let you repair errors without losing data. If not, Disk Utility will let you reformat, once again at the cost of wiping a drive clean.

One simpler possibility is that you need to update your hardware drivers. This is dead simple on macOS, since Apple typically bundles these in with the latest OS updates. Just head to Apple menu > System Settings > General > Software Update to check. In Windows 11, swing by Settings > Windows Update to install anything there.

In some cases, though, Windows users may need to return to the right-click Properties menu for a drive in Device Manager. Once you're there, click on the Driver tab, then try updating or uninstalling. If you uninstall without selecting the driver deletion option, restarting your PC should automatically reinstall the correct software, which might repair it.

If you've gotten this far without luck, there may not be much you can do other than cross your fingers that a reboot will solve things or seek out third-party help, such as the drive manufacturer or a repair shop. You might need a recovery firm's help if valuable data is trapped. You can also try your Mac or PC's general OS recovery tools, but these are unlikely to fix anything we haven't already suggested.

#306. Axes and cutlasses: Violence on Nigeria's election campaign trail

As Nigeria's January 2027 elections approach, political violence and thuggery at campaign rallies and town hall meetings raise concerns about voter safety.

Samuel Adebanjo had gone to the Oregun area of Lagos, the economic heartbeat of Nigeria, to cover a town hall meeting organized by the opposition party, the National Democratic Congress (NDC). But what was supposed to be a routine reporting assignment took a violent turn when a group of armed men stormed the venue and disrupted the gathering.

"I was at the entrance, taking photos of people entering the hall when some buses drove in and I heard a loud bang," Samuel recalled. Before he could process what was happening, the men began chasing supporters of the party with axes, cutlasses, and wooden planks, forcing many to flee for safety.

Adebanjo ran towards the parking lot, hoping to find somewhere to hide. But some of the attackers spotted him and gave chase. The journalist with the local newspaper, The Cable, was surrounded by five men who started hitting him to make him let go of his camera. Despite wearing a press jacket, they accused him of being the party's cameraman. "They wanted to collect the camera. I was struggling with them because I didn't want them to take it away. In the process, my middle finger was broken," he said.

During the struggle, one of the thugs raised his axe and struck it towards his wrist. "I used my hand to guard it. I was expecting blood. I never knew it landed on my wristwatch, and that's when it hit me that they're not joking, and that I had to let go of my equipment."

He was left in agonizing pain. By the time the violence subsided and he was taken to the hospital, he had sustained a broken middle finger and internal injuries around his ribs. The attack also left several other people injured and properties, including vehicles belonging to supporters of the party, destroyed.

As the January 16, 2027 general election inches closer, incidents like this are becoming increasingly common, as incumbent Bola Tinubu battles for re-election on a ticket that revolves around combating insecurity and resolving the country's biting economic crisis.

Adebanjo's experience is not an isolated incident. According to the National Peace Committee, 109 breaches of the National Peace Accord have been recorded across the country's 26 states and the federal capital, Abuja.

Between August 19, when the campaign kicked off in the West African country, and October 27, political violence and thuggery, as well as misinformation and disinformation, top the violations, accounting for 33 and 29 incidents respectively.

Campaign rallies, town hall meetings and other political events organized by parties have been marred by violence, threats and intimidation, prompting analysts to caution that rising violence could taint the credibility of the elections and discourage voter participation.

On November 15, a group of men attacked the campaign convoy of former Kano state governor and National Democratic Congress vice-presidential candidate Rabiu Kwankwaso during a visit to the Bichi area of Kano. Similar incidents were recorded in both Sokoto and Kebbi when former Vice President Atiku Abubakar took his campaign to the northwestern states.

Civil society groups, including Amnesty International, have condemned the spate of election-related violence and intimidation across the country, urging security agencies to bring perpetrators to book. President Tinubu has also condemned the rising incidents of violence at political events, warning that intimidation and political thuggery capable of disrupting public order would not be tolerated.

Political violence is not new to Nigeria; nearly all of the country's elections have been tainted by violence and intimidation, including the deadly post-election violence that followed the 2011 elections, where at least 800 people were killed over days of rioting in states across northern Nigeria.

Raheem Mutiu, a Nigerian researcher at Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED), a global organization that collects data on conflicts and political violence worldwide, told DW that the pattern ahead of the coming polls is shaping up to show "political groups more agitated and determined to win elections by all means."

Mutiu described the spate of violence since the campaign was flagged off as mind-boggling. "Within the period of two months, we have recorded over 30 politically linked attacks with 10 fatalities. But what this one points to is that politically linked attacks have become more frequent and geographically widespread ahead of the January 2027 general election," he said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The country's multiparty politics has entrenched a winner-takes-all system that fuels fierce competition among parties and, at times, a willingness to resort to violence. There's also a growing intolerance for opposition among party supporters, although perpetrators are difficult to identify because they often act anonymously and as proxies for the interests they support.

"What we have seen again is that supporters across the political spectrum are involved in the attacks, but intensity of their violence and engagement largely depends on their local stronghold and territorial dominance," Mutiu added.

A voter choosing under threat is not choosing freely, Dengiyefa Angalapu, a researcher at the Abuja-based Center for Democracy and Development, told DW. He noted that apart from the physical attacks, the spread of fake news and hate speech narratives, which form part of the non-physical breaches of the peace accord, "can deceive voters and undermine trust in genuine information."

Angalapu stressed that the growing threat of electoral violence could further undermine voter participation in a country already struggling with low turnout. More than 103 million Nigerians are registered to vote in the 2027 general elections, according to the country's electoral authority.

However, the country has consistently recorded low voter participation, with the 2023 general elections witnessing the lowest turnout since Nigeria's return to democratic rule in 1999. Only 27% of the nearly 94 million registered voters cast their ballots.

"Intimidation adds another pressure: someone who fears punishment for their political preference may avoid meetings or withdraw from politics altogether," Angalapu added.

Adebanjo is still recovering from his injuries. The attack has left him with a bigger question about safety ahead of the polls: "If this could happen to me, a journalist, how much more to the citizens? I am not sure, at this stage, people will even come out to vote."

"Creator earnings, AdSense payouts and YouTube Partner Program eligibility remain based on Qualified Views and Watch Hours."

#302. FAA suspends installation of router that led to a ground stop of flights across the US

The router malfunctioned and flooded other routers with data, prompting the FAA to order the ground stop.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has suspended the installation of a router model made by Hewlett-Packard Enterprise-owned Juniper Networks, which was part of its modernization efforts. As The New York Times reports, the agency believes the router played a major role in the issue that caused it to order a ground stop for all flights in the US on November 13. In addition to suspending new installations, it has also disabled more than 60 routers that had already been installed.

If you'll recall, Transport Secretary Sean Duffy blamed the ground stop on old hardware the first time he spoke about the event. But Duffy revealed a day later that the issue was connected to the modernization of America's aviation facilities.

He said a contractor from tech company L3Harris was working on switching telecommunication lines from old copper wires to fiber and on installing the new router at an FAA site in El Dorado, Arkansas. That router started flooding other routers in the air traffic control system with data. Another router in Amarillo, Texas had also gone haywire, and the FAA responded by disabling both of them.

The agency said the router was tested for a year before installations started. "Sixty-eight times it worked well," he sad at a news conference. "This one router started to broadcast into our network, and it started to overload the network." In aviation, routers are used to transmit data, including radar feeds, flight plans and weather information.

Despite knowing that it was the router that caused the issue, FAA administrator Bryan Bedford said they still don't know what triggered it. The Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee's Democratic members are urging the agency to find out why it had malfunctioned. They also asked the FAA to report to Congress on how it's going to prevent the same thing from happening in the future.

Duffy said he was told by national security agencies that the issue wasn't caused by a cyberattack, but he still asked the FBI to be part of the team analyzing the router from Arkansas. The Transport Secretary has also renewed his calls for Congress to approve an additional $50 billion in funding to modernize America's air traffic control system. "I would just tell you, the longer we stay on an old rickety network, the less safe it becomes," he said. "We do have to get this work done. Otherwise, staying on the old system for longer is going to mean more risk as opposed to fixing the system, and you're going to reduce the risk."

#300. Windows Server 2028 trades compatibility for out-of-the-box security

Hardened defaults align with DoD standards, but there may be growing pains.

Microsoft’s Ignite announcements this week went beyond the Office-in-Copilot overhaul with the reveal of the Windows Server 2028 Public Preview and its new security-by-default stance and what Microsoft calls Hardened Server Core. Windows Server 2028 will implement a default security framework that Microsoft says is aligned with hardened DoD benchmarks, such as the Defense Information Systems Agency’s (DISA) Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG).

STIGs work by providing a standard security framework for system administrators to follow recommended guidance. In the past, Windows Server admins were left to start from a blank canvas and then implement hardening configurations for operations. Secure baselines were available but not the default. Microsoft says that concern is now managed: “The secure configuration is the starting state, not a project you run after setup. That closes the window where a newly deployed server sits exposed while it waits to be hardened.”

The new Windows Server 2028 hardened-by-default state will only be available for the Server Core installs. Windows Server Desktop Experience installs do not include the changed stance.

This isn’t to say that system administrators won’t still have the final say on which security protocols are activated, just that the default package now ships in a pre-hardened state. Kerberos is now the default over NTLM, with protections added to LSASS; TLS is automatically restricted to modern cipher suites; key exchange uses “hybrid post-quantum key exchange” based on the quantum-safe ML-KEM; and remote desktop authentication and PowerShell script block logging get stricter as well.

Microsoft’s native NVMe storage stack was originally introduced via an update to Windows Server 2025, but it required administrators to enable it manually. The update eliminated NVMe translation through a SCSI stack while improving speeds and reducing overhead. The redesigned stack will now be default-on in Windows Server 2028.

Microsoft is upfront, noting that the new hardened security settings may break things due to software compatibility issues with older protocols, legacy authentication, or management tools and scripts. The company encourages users to try things and provide feedback about what goes wrong. “We want to hear where a hardened default gets in the way of a real workload: which setting, which application, and what you had to change to get it working,” the Windows Server Team said in a blog post. “That is how the defaults get better before general availability.”

Microsoft suggests that users use the preview build as a test bed to determine where issues like compatibility still arise. This is not a release candidate build and shouldn’t be treated as such. Despite the new security stance that comes with the preview build, hardware-backed protections like Secure Boot and DMA requirements won’t be enforced until a later preview build. Kerberos is now the default preference over NTLM, but NTLM blocking itself will still have to wait for a later preview release.

Beyond those limitations, the current build has a known issue that cuts into its hardened goals. According to the release notes, “A race condition in the TLS hybrid key exchange implementation may cause the LSASS service to crash when hybrid groups are negotiated by a TLS server.” Microsoft recommends disabling hybrid-key exchange groups until the problem is addressed.

System administrators and curious homelabbers interested in testing the new Windows Server 2028 can do so by registering with the Microsoft Windows Insider Program.

#298. The haunting Masters meltdown that changed Rory McIlroy's career

Editor’s Note:  This story was originally published in April 2023.

Slumped on his club, head buried in his arm, Rory McIlroy looked on the verge of tears.

The then-21-year-old had just watched his ball sink into the waters of Rae’s Creek at Augusta National and with it, his dream of winning The Masters, a dream that had looked so tantalizingly close mere hours earlier.

As a four-time major winner and one of the most decorated names in the sport’s history, few players would turn down the chance to swap places with McIlroy heading into Augusta this week.

Yet on Sunday afternoon of April 10, 2011, not a golfer in the world would have wished to be in the Northern Irishman’s shoes.

A fresh-faced, mop-headed McIlroy had touched down in Georgia for the first major of the season with a reputation as the leading light of the next generation of stars.

An excellent 2010 had marked his best season since turning pro three years earlier, highlighted by a first PGA Tour win at the Quail Hollow Championship and a crucial contribution to Team Europe’s triumph at the Ryder Cup.

Yet despite a pair of impressive top-three finishes at the Open and PGA Championship respectively, a disappointing missed cut at The Masters – his first at a major – served as ominous foreshadowing.

McIlroy shot 74 and 77 to fall four strokes short of the cut line at seven-over par, a performance that concerned him enough to take a brief sabbatical from competition.

But one year on in 2011, any lingering Masters demons looked to have been exorcised as McIlroy flew round the Augusta fairways.

Having opened with a bogey-free seven-under 65 – the first time he had ever shot in the 60s at the major – McIlroy pulled ahead from Spanish first round co-leader Alvaro Quirós with a second round 69.

It sent him into the weekend holding a two-shot cushion over Australia’s Jason Day, with Tiger Woods a further stroke behind and back in the hunt for a 15th major after a surging second round 66.

And yet the 21-year-old leader looked perfectly at ease with having a target on his back. Even after a tentative start to the third round, McIlroy rallied with three birdies across the closing six holes to stretch his lead to four strokes heading into Sunday.

The youngster was out on his own ahead of a bunched chasing pack comprising Day, Ángel Cabrera, K.J. Choi and Charl Schwartzel. After 54 holes, McIlroy had shot just three bogeys.

“It’s a great position to be in … I’m finally feeling comfortable on this golf course,” McIlroy told reporters.

“I’m not getting ahead of myself, I know how leads can dwindle away very quickly. I have to go out there, not take anything for granted and go out and play as hard as I’ve played the last three days. If I can do that, hopefully things will go my way.

“We’ll see what happens tomorrow because four shots on this golf course isn’t that much.”

The truth can hurt, and McIlroy was about to prove his assessment of Augusta to be true in the most excruciating way imaginable.

His fourth bogey of the week arrived immediately. Having admitted to expecting some nerves at the first tee, McIlroy sparked a booming opening drive down the fairway, only to miss his putt from five feet.

Three consecutive pars steadied the ship, but Schwartzel had the wind in his sails. A blistering birdie, par, eagle start had seen him draw level at the summit after his third hole.

A subsequent bogey from the South African slowed his charge, as McIlroy clung onto a one-shot lead at the turn from Schwartzel, Cabrera, Choi, and a rampaging Woods, who shot five birdies and an eagle across the front nine to send Augusta into a frenzy.

Despite his dwindling advantage and the raucous Tiger-mania din ahead of him, McIlroy had responded well to another bogey at the 5th hole, draining a brilliant 20-foot putt at the 7th to restore his lead.

The fist pump that followed marked the high-water point of McIlroy’s round, as a sliding start accelerated into full-blown free-fall at the par-four 10th hole.

His tee shot went careening into a tree, ricocheting to settle between the white cabins that separate the main course from the adjacent par-three course. It offered viewers a glimpse at a part of Augusta rarely seen on broadcast, followed by pictures of McIlroy anxiously peering out from behind a tree to track his follow-up shot.

Though his initial escape was successful, yet another collision with a tree and a two-putt on the green saw a stunned McIlroy eventually tap in for a triple bogey. Having led the field one hole and seven shots earlier, he arrived at the 11th tee in seventh.

By the time his tee drive at the 13th plopped into the creek, all thoughts of who might be the recipient of the green jacket had long-since switched away from the anguished youngster. It had taken him seven putts to navigate the previous two greens, as a bogey and a double bogey dropped him to five-under – the score he had held after just 11 holes of the tournament.

Mercifully, the last five holes passed without major incident. A missed putt for birdie from five feet at the final hole summed up McIlroy’s day, though he was given a rousing reception as he left the green.

Mere minutes earlier, the same crowd had erupted as Schwartzel sunk his fourth consecutive birdie to seal his first major title. After starting the day four shots adrift of McIlroy, the South African finished 10 shots ahead of him, and two ahead of second-placed Australian duo Jason Day and Adam Scott.

McIlroy’s eight-over 80 marked the highest score of the round. Having headlined the leaderboard for most of the week, he finished tied-15th.

Tears would flow during a phone call with his parents the following morning, but at his press conference, McIlroy was upbeat.

“I’m very disappointed at the minute, and I’m sure I will be for the next few days, but I’ll get over it,” he said.

“I was leading this golf tournament with nine holes to go, and I just unraveled … It’s a Sunday at a major, what it can do.

“This is my first experience at it, and hopefully the next time I’m in this position I’ll be able to handle it a little better. I didn’t handle it particularly well today obviously, but it was a character-building day … I’ll come out stronger for it.”

Once again, McIlroy would be proven right.

Just eight weeks later in June, McIlroy rampaged to an eight-shot victory at the US Open. Records tumbled in his wake at Congressional, as he shot a tournament record 16-under 268 to become the youngest major winner since Tiger Woods at The Masters in 1997.

The historic victory kickstarted a golden era for McIlroy. After coasting to another eight-shot win at the PGA Championship in 2012, McIlroy became only the third golfer since 1934 to win three majors by the age of 25 with triumph at the 2014 Open Championship.

Before the year was out, he would add his fourth major title with another PGA Championship win.

And much of it was owed to that fateful afternoon at Augusta. In an interview with the BBC in 2015, McIlroy dubbed it “the most important day” of his career.

“If I had not had the whole unravelling, if I had just made a couple of bogeys coming down the stretch and lost by one, I would not have learned as much.

“Luckily, it did not take me long to get into a position like that again when I was leading a major and I was able to get over the line quite comfortably. It was a huge learning curve for me and I needed it, and thankfully I have been able to move on to bigger and better things.

“Looking back on what happened in 2011, it doesn’t seem as bad when you have four majors on your mantelpiece.”

McIlroy’s contentment came with a caveat: it would be “unthinkable” if he did not win The Masters in his career.

Yet as he prepares for his 15th appearance at Augusta National this week, a green jacket remains an elusive missing item from his wardrobe.

Despite seven top-10 finishes in his past 10 Masters outings, the trophy remains the only thing separating McIlroy from joining the ranks of golf immortals to have completed golf’s career grand slam of all four majors in the modern era: Gene Sarazen, Ben Hogan, Gary Player, Jack Nicklaus, and Tiger Woods.

A runner-up finish to Scottie Scheffler last year marked McIlroy’s best finish at Augusta, yet arguably 2011 remains the closest he has ever been to victory. A slow start in 2022 meant McIlroy had begun Sunday’s deciding round 10 shots adrift of the American, who teed off for his final hole with a five-shot lead despite McIlroy’s brilliant 64 finish.

At 33 years old, time is still on his side. Though 2022 extended his major drought to eight years, it featured arguably his best golf since that golden season in 2014.

And as McIlroy knows better than most, things can change quickly at Augusta National.

#296. ICJ to rule on Rohingya genocide case against Myanmar: What to know

The ICJ is set to decide whether Myanmar's military operations in Rakhine State a decade ago were carried out with the intent to destroy the country's Rohingya minority, in whole or in part.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) will deliver on Thursday its long-awaited judgment in The Gambia's landmark genocide case against Myanmar, seven years after the case was lodged in The Hague.

The Gambia filed the case with the United Nations' top court in November 2019, formally accusing the Southeast Asian nation of breaking its obligations under the 1948 UN Genocide Convention.

In documents and hearings, The Gambia has alleged that Myanmar waged a deliberate campaign of arson, rape and murder in Rakhine State from 2016 to 2017, intending to wipe out the area's ethnic Rohingya minority, in whole or in part.

A UN fact-finding mission later concluded that some 10,000 people likely died in the pogroms. Another 700,000 Rohingya fled the country to neighboring Bangladesh, where most of them still live today in the world's largest refugee settlement.

Even before 2016, the predominantly Muslim Rohingya had been subjected to decades of persecution by the Buddhist-majority country's government, with many forced into resettlement camps and most denied citizenship.

A number of cases over Myanmar's treatment of the Rohingya have been filed in courts around the world. The ICJ will be the first to issue a ruling.

"The Rohingya people have been waiting for justice for decades for the atrocities and crimes committed against [us]. There were no venues available in [Myanmar]… International venues were the only hope," said Aung Kyaw Moe, a prominent Rohingya activist whose family was forced to flee the country during the pogroms.

"We've come over many years to a situation where a judgment will be delivered, and the expectation from the Rohingya community is very high," he said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A month after The Gambia lodged its case with the ICJ in 2019, Nobel laureate Aung San Suu Kyi, Myanmar's de facto civilian leader at the time, traveled to The Hague to contest the allegations, calling them "incomplete and incorrect."

The move tarnished her international reputation as a human rights icon. Many human rights advocates criticized her for defending the very military that had persecuted her for most of her life.

In 2020, ahead of a final judgment, the ICJ issued emergency "provisional measures" ordering Myanmar to take all steps "within its power" to prevent acts of genocide against the Rohingya, an order rights groups say it has blatantly ignored.

Myanmar's military went on to oust the country's democratically elected government the following year, placing Aung San Suu Kyi under arrest and setting off a bloody civil war that continues to rage.

Myanmar also challenged both the court's jurisdiction over the alleged crimes and The Gambia's right to lodge the case, both of which the ICJ rejected in 2022.

The ICJ then held 14 days of hearings this January for Myanmar and The Gambia to make their arguments before the panel. While Myanmar called one witness, The Gambia called three, as well as an expert.

As The Gambia has accused Myanmar of breaking several articles of the Genocide Convention, Thursday's judgment could be "fairly complicated," said Melanie O'Brien, a professor of international law at the University of Western Australia and past president of the International Association of Genocide Scholars.

The convention outlines that states have a duty to prevent and punish genocide and to establish effective penalties for those found responsible. The ICJ could rule in Myanmar's favor on some of these provisions and against it on others.

"So, there's quite a lot of layers here. They'll be looking at all of those issues, along with, of course, delving into the facts of the case and the individual crimes of genocide and whether or not Myanmar committed those individual crimes with the intent to destroy the Rohingya," O'Brien said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Proving Myanmar's intent behind the alleged atrocities is the key question the ICJ is grappling with.

Myanmar argues that its actions were strictly part of a legitimate counterinsurgency and counterterrorism operation, and that those actions could not at the same time be judged as acts of genocide.

Days before the Myanmar military launched its heaviest operations in Rakhine, in August 2017, the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army, an armed group based in the state, staged a coordinated attack on more than 30 police posts, killing several officers.

The Gambia argues that Myanmar's actions can qualify as both counterinsurgency and genocide at the same time. It also argues that the sexual violence and killing of children that accompanied the operations are proof that genocide was part of the goal.

"It directly undermines Myanmar's argument that this was a legitimate counterterrorism operation," said Michael Becker, an associate professor of international human rights law at Trinity College Dublin and a former associate legal officer at the ICJ.

"Because evidence of those types of atrocities are very hard to square with the idea that this had some other purpose beyond terrorizing the Rohingya population and indeed taking actions to try to destroy them," he said.

O'Brien and Becker said The Gambia's case against Myanmar is a chance for the ICJ to clarify how it weighs such circumstantial or indirect evidence when judging whether genocide has taken place.

Because investigators were denied access to Rakhine State, they had to rely on interviews with victims and witnesses who had fled Myanmar and on reports by the UN and other groups.

"And how the court deals with that, whether the ICJ accepts or rejects The Gambia's view or Myanmar's view of genocidal intent and how you prove it, this will have major repercussions for other cases," said Becker.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The ICJ is grappling with some of the same questions in cases between the Democratic Republic of Congo and Rwanda, Ukraine and Russia, and South Africa and Israel.

"I'm sure that the parties in the other cases will pick up on what the court rules in this case and add it to their own cases," said O'Brien.

"And even though this case will only be binding on The Gambia and Myanmar, the court itself may also refer to its own law in their future cases," she added.

The ICJ's judgment may have some effect on not only other cases but other courts as well.

The International Criminal Court — which, unlike the ICJ, tries individuals and not states — is considering an arrest warrant request for Myanmar coup leader Min Aung Hlaing in a trial on alleged crimes against humanity committed against the Rohingya. Becker and O'Brien say a finding of genocide by the ICJ could bolster the case for granting the warrant.

What a finding of genocide would actually do for the Rohingya is another key question.

Enforcing any reparations or restitution the court may order would rest with the UN Security Council. But with China and Russia, both allies of Min Aung Hlaing's regime, holding veto power on the council, there are serious doubts about whether it would act on any court order on Myanmar.

Aung Kyaw Moe remains hopeful that the Rohingya will one day receive justice.

"Despite these challenges, there are a lot of hopes that we can [move] toward the betterment of the Rohingya people, including compensation, reparations, transitional justice in the domestic setting in the long term," he said.

#295. NASA's Voyager 1 space probe is now one light-day away from Earth

It traveled more than 49 years to get to this point, and its journey isn’t done yet.

If NASA's estimates are correct, Voyager 1 is already one light-day away from our planet. NASA expects it to have reached that milestone at 5:16:07 AM Eastern time today, November 18. One light-day is the distance a particle of light can travel in a day. Since radio waves travel at the speed of light, it now takes 24 hours to send a command to the probe and 24 hours to get a message back. That's why NASA won't be able to confirm exactly what time it reached one light-day away until tomorrow, when the probe's message arrives.

"It's never happened before, and it may never happen again — it's that kind of extraordinary," said Voyager mission manager Kareem Badaruddin.

Voyager 1 headed to space in 1977 as part of NASA's program to study not just our Solar System, but also interstellar space. It was launched 16 days after Voyager 2, but it has since traveled farther than its twin and any other probe we've sent out. Voyager 1 reached interstellar space — that's the region between star systems — back in 2012, before Voyager 2 did. It suffered technical glitches, and NASA had to shut down some of its features to keep it going despite the diminishing plutonium in its generator. But it's still around and hasn't stopped its journey.

After traveling for 49 years, two months and 11 days, it's now believed to be about 16 billion miles from our planet—and it's not done yet. Voyager 1 is headed toward a star called Gliese 445, about 17 light-years from Earth in the Ursa Minor constellation. In terms of space distances, that's not so far away. However, none of us would be here by the time it reaches that goal: It's expected to pass within 1.7 light-years of Gliese 445 in 40,000 years.

#291. SiriusXM and Pandora will provide podcast transcripts for the deaf and hard-of-hearing community

This settles a lawsuit that goes all the way back to 2021.

SiriusXM has agreed to provide podcast transcripts for the deaf and hard-of-hearing community, as part of a legal settlement that resolves a lawsuit from 2021. The settlement impacts both SiriusXM and Pandora podcasts.

This won't be a slapdash affair. The transcripts must include speaker identification, any relevant atmospherics, sound effects, proper punctuation, paragraph breaks and just about everything else one would need to properly enjoy the content. The decree also requires human cleanup, so an actual person will have to review the transcripts if assisted by speech recognition algorithms.

The company will build custom data dictionaries of words and phrases specific to each podcast and develop an active style guide with input from the suit's plaintiffs. Finally, it must train staff on Deaf culture and communication access. All in all, this looks like a solid win for accessibility advocates.

"Podcasts have become a huge part of how we share news, ideas, stories and information, and deaf people deserve equal access to all of it," said plaintiff James Munro. "We hope this sparks even more change across the podcasting world. Let's make inaccessible podcasts a thing of the past!"

The original lawsuit was filed back in 2021. At that time, neither SiriusXM or Pandora offered podcast transcripts of any kind for the deaf and hard-of-hearing community. This was seen as a violation of the Americans with Disabilities Act.

There are still podcast platforms out there without robust transcription systems in place. Nick Kiego, CEO of the National Association of the Deaf, said that he hopes "this settlement will serve as a benchmark for other providers of podcast entertainment, opening the doors for deaf and hard of hearing people to fully access, engage in and enjoy the latest conversations in everything from politics to pop culture."
